title: Artificial intelligence in language instruction: impact on English learning achievement, L2 motivation, and self-regulated learning
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-mediated language instruction improves English learning outcomes, second-language (L2) motivation, and self-regulated learning among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. The study is framed as a response to growing interest in AI for education and specifically asks whether AI-supported instruction produces better outcomes than traditional language instruction, while also exploring students’ perceptions of the AI-supported experience.

The intervention was AI-mediated language instruction delivered through Duolingo. Students in the experimental group used Duolingo for interactive exercises, quizzes, language games, and real-time feedback during a 10-week instructional period, with at least 2 hours per week of additional out-of-class practice encouraged. The comparison group received traditional language instruction using textbooks, lectures, teacher-led discussions, grammar drills, reading passages, and writing exercises, also with at least 2 hours per week of outside practice. The study included pre- and post-tests for English achievement and questionnaires for L2 motivation and self-regulation, plus semi-structured interviews with a subset of students in the experimental group.

The participants were 60 undergraduate university students in mainland China enrolled in two intact EFL classes, all with intermediate English proficiency. The setting appears to be a university classroom context supplemented by platform use outside class. Fourteen students from the experimental group also participated in qualitative interviews about their experiences with the AI-mediated instruction.

The paper concludes that AI-mediated instruction had a significant positive effect on English learning achievement, L2 motivation, and self-regulated learning compared with traditional instruction. Quantitatively, the experimental group improved more than the control group on post-test English achievement and showed stronger gains in motivation and self-regulation. Qualitatively, students described the AI platform as engaging, personalized, motivating, confidence-building, and supportive of autonomous learning. Although the paper mentions ChatGPT and other AI tools in the literature review, the actual intervention studied was Duolingo rather than ChatGPT, and it does not provide a direct comparison of ChatGPT-generated writing feedback versus legacy automated writing tools or other secondary writing-feedback systems.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods quasi-experimental study with pre/post comparison groups and reported reliability for instruments, but it is not a K-12 study, uses only two intact university classes, and lacks a direct randomized controlled comparison of ChatGPT-generated feedback versus established secondary writing tools.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported quantitative effects are large on composite achievement and moderate-to-large on motivation and self-regulation (partial η² values up to 0.81), indicating substantial positive impact within the studied university EFL context, though relevance to the high-school ChatGPT-writing-feedback topic is low.

interventions.use_case: Duolingo-based AI-mediated English instruction for university EFL learners, providing app-based interactive exercises, quizzes, language games, and real-time personalized feedback over a 10-week intervention.
Personalized English language instruction through Duolingo adapting content and feedback to learner performance in grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing practice.
Software-delivered language practice used as the treatment condition versus traditional teacher-led instruction, with interactive digital exercises supplementing classwork.

finding.finding_summary: In this 10-week quasi-experimental study of 60 university EFL learners, the AI-mediated Duolingo group improved more than the traditional instruction group on overall English achievement, which included reading comprehension and writing as assessed components. Post-test overall achievement means were 73.86 (SD=15.26) for the experimental group versus 61.11 (SD=14.97) for controls; the mixed-design ANOVA showed a significant Group effect, F(1,58)=94.35, p<0.001, partial η²=0.81, and a significant Group×Time interaction, F(1,58)=8.37, p<0.001, partial η²=0.23, although no literacy-only effect size was separately reported.
finding.measure: English achievement test including reading comprehension and writing components
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.81 (group effect); partial eta squared=0.23 (group×time interaction)
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post-test SD=15.26; Control post-test SD=14.97

finding.finding_summary: The AI-mediated instruction group showed higher L2 motivation after 10 weeks than the traditional instruction group, with post-test means of 3.89 (SD=1.8) versus 3.35 (SD=1.5). Mixed-design ANOVA indicated a significant Time effect, F(1,58)=34.10, p<0.001, partial η²=0.44, and a significant Group×Time interaction, F(1,58)=7.43, p=0.04, partial η²=0.11, suggesting greater motivational gains under the AI condition.
finding.measure: 16-item L2 motivation scale assessing attitude, self-confidence, and personal use
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.11 (group×time interaction); partial eta squared=0.44 (time effect)
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post-test SD=1.8; Control post-test SD=1.5

finding.finding_summary: AI-mediated instruction was associated with stronger gains in self-regulated learning than traditional instruction in the sample of 60 university EFL learners. Post-test self-regulation scores were 3.94 (SD=0.73) for the Duolingo group and 3.37 (SD=0.76) for controls, with significant ANOVA effects for Group, F(1,58)=11.36, p<0.001, partial η²=0.64, Time, F(1,48)=8.94, p<0.001, partial η²=0.24, and Group×Time, F(1,58)=7.68, p<0.001, partial η²=0.38.
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.38 (group×time interaction); partial eta squared=0.64 (group effect)
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post-test SD=0.73; Control post-test SD=0.76

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames English learning achievement broadly and reports significant gains for the AI-mediated group on a composite test including grammar and vocabulary, which are relevant to language proficiency, but it does not report separate speaking or listening outcomes. Thus, evidence for language fluency is indirect and limited to overall language achievement improvements in n=60 learners.
finding.measure: Composite English achievement test with grammar and vocabulary components
finding.effect_size: partial eta squared=0.81 (overall group effect on composite achievement)
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post-test SD=15.26; Control post-test SD=14.97
